newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Delaying EMU could trigger major overhaul.
newsitem.headline: Delaying EMU could trigger major overhaul.

text.p: Stopping the clock to delay the launch of a single European currency could open a constitutional Pandora's Box and force the renegotiation of the Maastricht Treaty and its EMU criteria, EU officials fear.

While Germany and others have rushed to quash market rumours that the Bundesbank or German finance ministry was about to announce a two-year delay in economic and monetary union (EMU), talk of slippage is in the air.

The feeling remains that Germany's difficulties in meeting EMU criteria, partly because of record post-war unemployment, plus fears in Frankfurt and Bonn that undeserving countries might make the EMU grade, increasingly point towards some kind of delay.

"Having formerly believed in a grand EMU fudge should Germany overshoot its fiscal targets, the market is currently adjusting to the possibility that Germany would prefer to delay EMU rather than proceed on a flawed basis," according to Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
EU officials, denying that any delay is even being considered, note that triggering a delay would pose big problems.

"If you did want to change the date from January 1, 1999, that would imply changing the treaty, which would involve all the procedures of negotiation and ratification by national governments," one said.
The gist is that EMU and the qualification criteria are enshrined in a treaty.
Changing any part of that would require EU member states to meet, agree unanimously on how to proceed, and get 15 national governments to go along.
The European Commission, the official guardian of EU treaties, fears that could prompt wholescale tinkering.
"The view is that once that process is launched, monetary union would not simply be delayed by one or two years but the whole thing would be put off for many years," the official said.
European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy believes a delay could lead to mayhem in the markets.

"I am sure that if we have to postpone it would be the end of monetary union. The result in economic terms would be dreadful. The message to financial markets will be that member states don't want to reduce their excessive deficits and don't want lower inflation rates," he told Britain's Guardian newspaper in an interview published on Tuesday.

Although there would be nothing to stop Germany, or any other country, saying it wanted to delay EMU, the prospect of a treaty renegotiation may be sufficient to stop any such move, some analysts believe.
Daniel Gros, director of economic issues at the Centre for European Studies, said it was "far-fetched" to think Germany was trying now to delay EMU.
But he did not rule some kind of technical postponment of a few months to allow a few straggling economies to catch up.
Were a delay to be on the cards, he said, it would be far more likely to be early in 1998 when EU members meet to decide which among them have qualified for EMU.
"At that point the option of a technical postponement would look possible," he said.

Under this scenario, the EU could stick with its treaty, have the new European Central Bank begin work on schedule in January 1999, but delay the technical introduction of a single currency for a few months to allow some members to get their 1998 budgets into line.,
